segments.title: Tiger's hull makes a 15-inch refit physically plausible
segments.body: The counterfactual begins with ship geometry and the space required for heavier guns. Tiger's 13.5-inch barbettes were about 24 feet 6 inches across, while the 15-inch Mark I mounting required roughly 30 feet, so the supporting structure needed to grow by about 2 feet 9 inches on every side. The comparison then turns to Tiger's beam and displacement density alongside the Queen Elizabeth class, Renown, and Hood. Tiger scores much closer to ships already carrying 15-inch guns than to the more lightly built Renown. The calculation does not make the conversion easy, but it gives a concrete reason to regard the hull as strong and spacious enough for serious study.

evidence.note: Compares the 13.5-inch and 15-inch barbette diameters and calculates the extra width required.
Uses beam and displacement-density comparisons to argue that Tiger's hull could support the larger armament.

segments.summary: Barbette diameters, beam, and displacement density turn the proposed 15-inch rearmament into a testable naval-architecture problem.

segments.title: Tiger approaches the fast battleship from the battlecruiser side
segments.body: Tiger represents one side of a British design convergence toward the fast battleship. Battlecruisers develop toward Tiger while battleships develop toward the Queen Elizabeth class, producing ships that solve similar speed-and-protection problems from different starting points. Hood looks denser on a simple displacement calculation, but much of her protection was added after Jutland while she was already under construction. Tiger's internal structure was designed as a coherent, heavily built package from the outset. The comparison shows how labels can conceal the fast-battleship qualities of some late battlecruisers.

evidence.note: Describes battlecruiser and battleship development as two British routes toward the fast battleship.
Contrasts Tiger's purpose-built density with protection added to Hood after Jutland.

segments.summary: Tiger and the Queen Elizabeth class represent two British routes toward combining battle-line strength with high speed.

segments.title: Tiger's speed and stability reflect pressure from foreign battlecruisers
segments.body: Tiger's official speed was 28 knots, but her fully laden trials reached about 29.5 knots despite coal-and-oil firing and a curious arrangement of 39 boilers. Full oil firing could plausibly have pushed her toward 30 knots. A strong metacentric height also made her a notably stable gun platform. Although only slightly longer and wider than Queen Mary, Tiger was roughly 2,000 tons heavier and represented a materially different design. British observation of German construction, Japan's Kongo-class orders, and faster battle-line concepts increased the likelihood of battles between fast heavy ships and help explain the extra investment.

evidence.note: Covers trials speed, boiler pressure, oil firing, the 39-boiler layout, and metacentric stability.
Compares Tiger with Queen Mary and links the design to German ships, Japan's Kongo class, and rising battle-line speeds.

segments.summary: Trials performance and construction distinguish Tiger from Queen Mary and show how foreign battlecruisers influenced the design.

segments.title: Jutland supplies combat evidence for Tiger's resilience
segments.body: The Battle of Jutland turns Tiger's strength from a design claim into operational evidence. She was hit by fifteen 11-inch shells, at least two 12-inch shells, and several 5.9-inch rounds. Damage affected her belt area, flare stores, sick bay, cable spaces, and a funnel, yet the ship survived and returned to service quickly. That record does not prove that every reconstruction choice would work, but it does show a resilient structure capable of absorbing severe punishment. The example helps explain why the Royal Navy still valued Tiger when treaty negotiations began.

evidence.note: Enumerates Tiger's shell hits and damaged spaces at Jutland.
Emphasizes the ship's survival, resilience, and rapid return to service.

segments.summary: Tiger's heavy shell damage and rapid return to service provide a wartime test of the hull strength assumed by the refit scenario.

segments.title: Washington treaty rules block the historical Tiger gun change
segments.body: Technical feasibility and treaty permission were separate questions. The reconstruction rules permitted bulges, blisters, anti-aircraft protection, and up to 3,000 tons of defensive additions. They barred changes to side armor and to the caliber, number, or general mounting type of a retained capital ship's main armament, except for specified French, Italian, and British cases. Tiger would remain below the 35,000-ton standard-displacement ceiling and the 16-inch gun limit even after a substantial rebuild. The specific ban on changing the main battery explains why the conversion did not happen historically.

evidence.note: Reads the treaty's defensive-reconstruction allowance and prohibition on main-armament changes.
Explains that Tiger met the overall tonnage and caliber limits but failed the reconstruction rule.

segments.summary: Tiger fits the treaty's broad tonnage and caliber ceilings, but the reconstruction clause forbids changing her main-gun caliber or mounting type.

segments.title: Stored Courageous turrets show Britain's measured rearmament pace
segments.body: Britain did not need to design every part of a Tiger rearmament from scratch. The 15-inch guns and turrets removed during the Courageous-class carrier conversions were stored, leaving the main hardware for an eight-gun ship available. Britain also held armor plate in reserve and was willing to buy specialist material abroad. If political leaders had believed that emergency rearmament justified any expense, they could have used these assets to pursue a Vanguard-like capital ship much earlier. Their choice supports a reading of British rearmament as a measured political and economic response, despite greater urgency within the armed forces.

evidence.note: Identifies the stored Courageous-class turrets and explains why hull strength matters when carrying armor.
Uses stored guns and armor-supply options to characterize British rearmament as politically measured.

segments.summary: Stored 15-inch mountings from the Courageous-class conversions provide the hardware for an eight-gun ship and weaken claims of panicked rearmament.

segments.title: Tiger's strategic speed could put heavy guns at Singapore in time
segments.body: Tiger's 1918 refit and continued retention make sense when viewed through the Royal Navy's worldwide response problem. British political and economic thinking treated the empire as a national necessity, leaving much of its Far Eastern defense to the navy. At a crisis cruising speed near 24 knots, a fast squadron could reach Singapore from Portsmouth in about fourteen days or from Malta in roughly ten. Those times compare favorably with a possible Japanese movement from Sasebo once warning from mobilization is included, while an 18-to-21-knot battle fleet might be too late. The immediate aim was deterrence: place visible power in the region while the crisis was still developing and before the larger fleet arrived.

evidence.note: Introduces Tiger's 1918 refit and compares fast-squadron transit times from Portsmouth and Malta with the battle fleet.
Relates Japanese mobilization warning to Singapore timing and describes the fast ships as a deterrent rapid-response force.

segments.summary: Transit-time arithmetic shows why fast capital ships served as a deterrent and rapid-response force for Britain's Far Eastern commitments.

segments.title: The London treaty removes Tiger before her replacement is ready
segments.body: Tiger remained in commission until 1931 under her final captain, Arthur Bedford. Her withdrawal followed the London Naval Treaty and British plans to free tonnage for the next generation of capital ships. The replacement program then suffered repeated delays before work began on the King George V class. Tiger was sold for breaking in 1932, although accounts differ on when physical dismantling started. Treaty accounting had therefore removed an existing capability well before its planned replacement reached the fleet.

evidence.note: Connects Tiger's 1931 withdrawal with the London treaty, replacement tonnage, and delays to the King George V class.
Dates the sale for breaking and notes uncertainty over when dismantling actually began.

segments.summary: Tiger left service in 1931 as treaty tonnage was cleared for a new generation, but delays postponed the King George V class and left a capability gap.

segments.title: Third Sea Lords connect Tiger to worldwide task-group operations
segments.body: A workable counterfactual needs a plausible reason for policy to change, and this one begins with the Third Sea Lords who could turn strategic need into ship-design policy. Frederick Field held the post long enough to develop a worldwide vision and favored the fast F3 concept over the slower N3 because a future war might be fought far from Britain. An ideal force arriving late is operationally useless, while permanent forward deployment would require far more ships and money. Battlecruisers were an interim answer until machinery achieved the power density needed for a fully armored fast battleship. Ernle Chatfield and Roger Backhouse also appear as officers thinking about dispersed task groups that would need strategic speed to maneuver and support one another across the globe.

evidence.note: Explains that the counterfactual needs a logical mechanism and identifies the Third Sea Lords as the starting point.
Introduces the Third Sea Lords, Field's preference for F3, global force projection, and the machinery tradeoff behind battlecruisers.
Discusses Chatfield, Backhouse, dispersed task groups, mutual support, and strategic speed.

segments.summary: Frederick Field, Ernle Chatfield, and Roger Backhouse supply the institutional case for fast capital ships able to reinforce dispersed forces.

segments.title: A 15-inch standardization bargain changes the treaty path
segments.body: Two political routes could bypass the historical restriction. Britain could claim that Tiger's conversion was already under way and seek treatment similar to Renown, or it could give up 16-inch ambitions in exchange for standardizing future capital ships on the 15-inch gun. Standardization would simplify fleet logistics while surrendering little practical striking power. Either route depends on securing language in the Washington settlement, since the technical case alone could not override the reconstruction rules.

evidence.note: Sets out the 15-inch standardization bargain and the alternative claim that reconstruction was already in progress.

segments.summary: Britain could seek either an exemption for work already begun or a treaty bargain that traded 16-inch prestige for 15-inch fleet commonality.

segments.title: Standard displacement hides Tiger's full-load scale
segments.body: The treaty allowance adds 3,000 tons to Tiger's declared 28,500-ton standard displacement, but that figure does not describe a fully loaded ship. The transcript assigns about 7,000 tons to coal and fuel oil alone, then adds feed water to estimate roughly 39,000 to 40,000 tons at full load. It also cautions that treaty declarations gave Britain an incentive to keep the stated standard figure low, so the precise baseline should be treated carefully. Even on the declared figure, a rebuilt Tiger would exceed the standard displacement of the Queen Elizabeth and R classes and remain below Hood. The arithmetic shows why standard and full-load displacement answer different questions.

evidence.note: Adds the 3,000-ton allowance to Tiger's declared standard displacement, then estimates full load from fuel, coal, and feed water while cautioning about treaty declarations.
Compares a rebuilt Tiger's declared standard displacement with Hood, the Queen Elizabeth class, and the R class.

segments.summary: Treaty figures omit fuel and feed water, so Tiger's declared 28,500 tons can coexist with an estimated 39,000 to 40,000 tons at full load.

segments.title: New boilers reshape Tiger's machinery layout
segments.body: The proposed rebuild changes far more than the gun mountings. Converting Tiger to all-oil firing would release coal-bunker space, while new boilers and possibly geared turbines would permit a major rearrangement of the machinery rooms and funnels. Tiger's 39 older water-tube boilers produced 85,000 shaft horsepower, while the eight higher-pressure Admiralty three-drum boilers in Nelson and Rodney produced 45,000 horsepower. On that rough power-density basis, about sixteen modern boilers could give Tiger roughly 90,000 horsepower while occupying far less space. The result might sustain about 29.5 knots or approach 30, improve the secondary-gun layout, and make the modernization a whole-ship engineering project rather than a turret exchange.

evidence.note: Sketches the funnel, oil-firing, bunker, secondary-gun, turbine, and boiler changes.
Compares Tiger's 39 boilers with Nelson and Rodney's plant and estimates the rebuilt ship's power and speed.

segments.summary: Oil firing and Nelson-era boilers could replace Tiger's 39-boiler plant with a much smaller, more powerful arrangement while freeing internal and deck space.

segments.title: Armor coverage matters alongside maximum thickness
segments.body: Tiger carried a 9-inch belt, about half again as thick as the principal protection on Renown and Repulse but below Hood's 12-inch maximum. Maximum thickness alone does not settle which ship had the better scheme because Tiger's belt covered a different proportion of the hull. Her armor was integrated into the design from the beginning, whereas much of Hood's additional protection entered after construction had started. Tiger also had up to 3 inches of deck armor, and her existing 8-to-9-inch barbettes would be replaced as part of the main-gun conversion. The final protection package would depend on whether the political route allowed an agreed pre-treaty rebuild or secured broader concessions during negotiations.

evidence.note: Compares Tiger's belt, armor coverage, deck armor, and barbettes with Renown, Repulse, and Hood.
Links the achievable protection changes to the two proposed treaty routes.

segments.summary: Tiger's 9-inch belt and original structural integration offer a different protection tradeoff from Hood's thicker but later-added armor.

segments.title: Rebuilding Tiger buys time and completes a four-ship fast force
segments.body: In the first scenario, Tiger's reconstruction begins in 1918 to preserve a useful fast capital ship while the Admiral class and successor designs remain unsettled. The Royal Navy wanted Courageous and Glorious out of the battle line quickly, but Tiger was its newest purpose-built battlecruiser and had spent most of the war operating near home maintenance facilities. Hard wartime service did not make a major rebuild unreasonable: Warspite was launched in November 1913, Tiger followed in December, and Warspite remained worth keeping in service. Retaining Tiger alongside Hood, Renown, and Repulse would create a four-ship fast force, enough in a standard force-generation model to keep one deployed, one training or transiting, one in light work, and one in major refit. Oil firing could also improve range, while eight 15-inch guns would give Tiger status and combat weight beyond the six-gun Renown and Repulse.

evidence.note: Frames the refit as a bridge to future ships and compares Tiger's age and service condition with Warspite.
Explains four-hull force generation, the resulting gun balance, improved endurance, prestige use, and possible bow changes.

segments.summary: A 1918 reconstruction could bridge the gap to new designs and give the Royal Navy four fast capital ships for a sustainable deploy-train-refit cycle.

segments.title: Accepting Tiger may be cheaper than reopening the treaty bargain
segments.body: The treaty system often accepted work and ships that already existed, as the special treatment of Renown and Hood illustrates. Refusing Tiger could prompt Britain to leave the agreement or demand authority for a third new 16-inch capital ship, worsening the tonnage arithmetic for other powers. Allowing one more 15-inch reconstruction could therefore become the least disruptive compromise. Britain would then enter the Second World War with four fast 15-inch capital ships. Tiger could cover assignments that historically fell to Hood, making it easier to send Hood into her planned modernization and changing which assets were available when war began.

evidence.note: Explains treaty acceptance of the status quo and the alternatives Britain could demand if Tiger were refused.
Traces the effect of a fourth fast ship on Tiger's employment and Hood's modernization schedule.

segments.summary: Treaty partners might tolerate a conversion already under way rather than risk British withdrawal or a demand for another new capital ship.

segments.title: Treaty tonnage could produce three or four F3-style capital ships
segments.body: The more ambitious scenario treats 15-inch standardization as a bargaining asset instead of an exemption confined to Tiger. After removing the four 13.5-inch battleships, Britain retained a little over 136,000 tons of capital-ship allowance. That was enough on paper for four ships near 34,000 tons, although three would be a more likely negotiated maximum. Even three F3-style ships, added to four battlecruisers, five Queen Elizabeths, and five R-class battleships, would create an unusually large and fast capital fleet.

evidence.note: Calculates the remaining British treaty allowance and the possible three- or four-ship F3 program.

segments.summary: Giving up 16-inch guns could let Britain use its remaining treaty allowance for a larger family of fast 15-inch ships derived from F3 thinking.

segments.title: Tiger could test a 15-inch/50 before the F2 and F3 ships
segments.body: A rebuilt Tiger could test a proposed 15-inch/50 weapon before that armament entered new capital ships. The F2 and F3 concepts were described as fully armored battlecruisers because their protection covered more of the hull, although their subdivision still followed battlecruiser standards. They continued the design path already visible in Tiger, approaching the fast battleship from the battlecruiser side. Tiger would therefore serve as an experimental bridge between an immediate refit and the next generation of British capital ships.

evidence.note: Suggests Tiger as a 15-inch/50 test ship and describes F2 and F3 as continuations of battlecruiser development toward the fast battleship.

segments.summary: Using rebuilt Tiger as a gun test bed links the immediate conversion to British work on fully armored battlecruisers and fast battleships.

segments.title: Two battle lines give Britain worldwide task-group depth
segments.body: A fleet with four F3s and four older battlecruisers would possess something close to two distinct battle lines. The conventional battle fleet could hold concentrated positions while fast ships formed task groups able to move between theaters. Availability matters as much as the headline total: the larger pool makes it realistic to have several fast capital ships at sea and several more ready in port despite training and refit demands. Even the less expansive seven-ship version would generate substantial deployable strength. The difference between 15-inch and 16-inch guns matters less in this argument than the number of heavy, fast hulls an opponent must account for.

evidence.note: Describes two battle lines and the Royal Navy's capacity to generate worldwide task groups.
Connects a seven- or eight-ship fast force with availability, deterrence, and the limited practical difference between 15-inch and 16-inch hits.

segments.summary: Seven or eight fast capital ships create a second operational battle line with enough depth for simultaneous deployment, maintenance, and deterrence.

segments.title: Fleet depth supports faster Queen Elizabeth refits and live raider exercises
segments.body: A deeper fast force creates schedule room for more refits, including a different Queen Elizabeth modernization aimed at additional speed. It also supplies a capital ship that can maneuver freely as the raider during exercises. Hunting such a target would test scouting and interception against a ship trying to evade at maximum speed. Those exercises could improve preparation for wartime searches for commerce raiders.

evidence.note: Links additional fleet depth to more refits, faster Queen Elizabeth modernizations, and exercises against a freely maneuvering high-speed raider.

segments.summary: More fast hulls free older ships for speed-focused modernization and give training fleets realistic high-speed raiders to hunt.

segments.title: A larger fast fleet undermines the German Panzerschiff concept
segments.body: Panzerschiffe retain some logic against Soviet or French forces, although Dunkerque already weakens the French case. Against Britain, Hood, Renown, and Repulse posed a serious existing risk. Adding Tiger and several fast Nelson- or F3-derived ships greatly expands the number of hunters able to catch and outclass German surface raiders. That change could push German planners away from the Panzerschiff concept before the Second World War.

evidence.note: Argues that numerous fast British capital ships make Panzerschiffe less viable and could redirect German development.

segments.summary: Tiger and several fast Nelson- or F3-derived ships would multiply the British hunters able to catch and outgun German Panzerschiffe.

segments.title: Fast battleships alter Mediterranean operations and Denmark Strait
segments.body: Faster Nelson-derived ships would spend less time guarding fixed choke points such as Gibraltar. With more high-speed capital ships available, British commanders could accept greater operational risk and bring heavier forces to battles such as Matapan. A 15-inch standard might also reshape the later King George V class, potentially avoiding some difficulties associated with the historical quadruple turrets. Greater availability could produce a different force at the Denmark Strait and other operations where strategic speed determined which ships could participate. The operational benefit comes from adding deployable speed across the fleet rather than relying on a few exceptional ships.

evidence.note: Discusses Gibraltar, Matapan, possible King George V armament changes, Denmark Strait, and strategic speed.

segments.summary: A larger pool of 28-knot capital ships changes where Britain can accept risk and which heavy units can reach time-sensitive operations.

segments.title: A 24-knot fast force raises the carrier speed requirement
segments.body: The capital-ship counterfactual reaches carrier design because fleet components must operate together. A traditional battle line progresses at about 18 knots, while this fast force would make at least 24. Carriers assigned to it would need enough speed to remain with the formation and provide support. The requirement ties battleship standardization to naval aviation instead of treating the carrier program in isolation.

evidence.note: Explains why carriers would need to keep pace with a fast capital-ship formation progressing at roughly 24 knots rather than an 18-knot battle line.

segments.summary: Carriers supporting the fast capital ships must keep pace with a formation advancing near 24 knots instead of the traditional 18-knot battle line.

segments.title: An eighteenth capital ship could support an Eastern battle squadron
segments.body: Britain could reach eighteen capital ships because its retained ships averaged about 27,782 tons once the 13.5-inch ships and Nelson and Rodney were set aside, well below the 35,000-ton individual ceiling. That total could support an additional battle squadron, which then raises the question of where to base it. Direct basing at Singapore becomes less attractive once Fascist Italy and Mediterranean tension demand flexibility closer to the Suez route. Trincomalee in Ceylon or a base on India's west coast would signal a visible commitment to Australia, New Zealand, and Britain's Eastern possessions. Ships stationed there could also move through the Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Suez Canal to reinforce the Mediterranean from an unexpected direction. The basing choice connects imperial defense with European war planning.

evidence.note: Calculates the eighteen-ship fleet and proposes forming another battle squadron.
Considers Trincomalee or western India as bases able to support both Eastern commitments and rapid movement toward the Mediterranean.

segments.summary: Ceylon or western India offers a politically Eastern but operationally flexible base for the extra squadron created by a larger treaty fleet.
